extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of improvisational comedy and television
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the format, rules-of-play, and notable variations/adaptations of the short-form improvisational comedy show Whose Line Is It Anyway? across radio and television versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel of four performers
rubrics_metrics.description: The show consists of a panel of four performers who create characters, scenes, and songs on the spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This core cast configuration is the basic unit of the show's format: performers improvise together in short-form games to produce scenes and musical numbers during an episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-form improvisation games
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes are built in the style of short-form improvisation games, many taken from theatresports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games are discrete, bounded improvisational formats (often with specific rules or constraints) used to generate comedy quickly; the page notes that many of the show's games derive from theatresports traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics from audience suggestions or predetermined prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics for the games are based on either audience suggestions or predetermined prompts from the host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompts can be solicited live from the audience or provided by the host in advance; the source of prompts is a defining feature of how scenes are seeded and how spontaneity is produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game-show framing with arbitrary scoring and winner
rubrics_metrics.description: The show ostensibly takes the form of a game show, with the host arbitrarily assigning points and likewise choosing a winner at the end of each episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring is part of the performative framing and not a formal competition; the arbitrary nature of points and the winner selection emphasize entertainment over genuine adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of production and cast across versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple versions (radio, British TV, American TV, and other international adaptations) were produced by the show's creators and exhibit continuity of cast and format elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that production continuity (same creators/producers) and recurring performers link different versions, which affects authenticity and recognizability across adaptations (e.g., some British performers appearing on the U.S. series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptations may modify games and target audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptations and international versions often retain many games from the original but may introduce new games or alter emphasis to suit different audiences (e.g., a version aimed at children, a hip-hop variant, team-based competitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include Sponk! (aimed at younger audiences with child performers), Wild 'n Out (hip-hop version with guest stars), and shows that split contestants into teams or emphasize acting over wild comedy. This indicates an evaluative/production principle: adaptations are judged by how they balance fidelity to core games with changes for local/audience needs.
